entry: Edible fruit of several *Rubus* species in the [[Rosaceae|rose family]]. Raspberries are perennial with woody stems. Each raspberry is an aggregate fruit formed from numerous drupelets, each containing a seed; a single fruit is made up of around 100 drupelets and weighs 3–5 g. Unlike [[Blackberry|blackberries]], where the torus stays with the fruit when picked, the raspberry's torus remains on the plant, leaving a hollow core. The plants thrive in well-drained soil with a pH between 6 and 7 and ample sun and water, though excess [[Irrigation|irrigation]] can bring on Phytophthora root rot. World production in 2023 was 940,979 tonnes, led by Russia with 23% of the total. The red raspberry (*Rubus idaeus*) is the most commonly associated species, and the fruit is eaten fresh or in preserves, cakes, pastries and ice cream. Black raspberries (*Rubus occidentalis*) are native to eastern North America and have a deeper flavor.

Abrahamic [[New religious movement|new religious movement]] that developed in [[Jamaica]] during the 1930s. Its beliefs are based on an interpretation of the [[Bible]] and center on a monotheistic God called Jah, who partly resides within each individual. Adherents accord key importance to [[Haile Selassie]], Emperor of Ethiopia between 1930 and 1974; many see him as the [[Second Coming]] of Jesus and Jah incarnate, while others regard him as a human prophet. Rastafari is Afrocentric and holds that the African diaspora is oppressed within "Babylon," meaning Western capitalist society. Many call for its resettlement in Africa, which they regard as Zion. Practices called "livity" include an Ital diet, dreadlocks and the use of [[Cannabis (drug)|cannabis]] as a sacrament at communal meetings called groundations. The movement was influenced by [[Marcus Garvey]]'s Back-to-Africa ideas, and [[Bob Marley]] popularized it through reggae in the 1960s and 1970s. Rastafari has no central authority, and estimates of its adherents range from 700,000 to 1 million worldwide.

Medium-sized, long-tailed [[Rodent|rodent]], most familiar in the genus *Rattus*. Rats belong to the same subfamily as [[Mouse|mice]] and are often distinguished by size. Of the 56 known species, the best-known are the black rat and the [[Brown rat|brown rat]], both native to [[Asia]]. Common species are commensal, living with and near humans, and can cause substantial food losses, especially in developing countries. Many other species are island endemics, some endangered by habitat loss or competition. Rats are found in every region inhabited by humans, excluding [[Antarctica]]. The [[Black Death]] is traditionally believed to have been caused by *Yersinia pestis*, carried by [[Flea|rat fleas]] that preyed on black rats in European cities during the epidemic outbreaks of the Middle Ages. The hairless, thin-skinned tail is highly vascularized, allowing efficient heat exchange with the environment. Rats become sexually mature at age 6 weeks but reach social maturity at about 5 to 6 months.

Number that can be expressed as the quotient or [[Fraction|fraction]] p/q of two [[Integer|integers]], with a nonzero denominator q. Every integer is rational. The rationals are closed under [[Addition|addition]], [[Subtraction|subtraction]], [[Multiplication|multiplication]] and [[Division (mathematics)|division]] by a nonzero rational, and form a field under these operations. A rational number is a real number whose decimal expansion either terminates, as 3/4 = 0.75, or eventually repeats a finite sequence of digits, as 9/44 = 0.20454545... This holds in every integer base, including binary and hexadecimal. Real numbers that are not rational are [[Irrational number|irrational]], including the square root of 2, [[Pi|π]] and e. The rationals are countable, while the real numbers are uncountable, so almost all real numbers are irrational. Every rational number can be written uniquely as an irreducible fraction a/b, with coprime integers and b > 0.

Epistemological view that reason is the chief source and test of knowledge, often in contrast to faith, tradition or sensory experience. During the Enlightenment, rationalism, sometimes equated with innatism, was opposed to [[Empiricism|empiricism]]. Rationalists such as [[René Descartes]] held that knowledge is primarily innate and that the intellect can directly grasp logical truths. They held that principles in [[Mathematics|mathematics]], logic, ethics and metaphysics are so fundamentally true that denying them causes contradiction. Empiricists such as [[John Locke]] argued that knowledge is best gained through sensory observation. Continental rationalism, associated with Descartes, [[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz|Leibniz]] and [[Baruch Spinoza|Spinoza]], applied mathematical methods to philosophy. Spinoza and Leibniz held that all knowledge could in principle be gained by reason alone, though in practice this was possible only in areas such as mathematics.

Venomous pit viper of the genera *Crotalus* and *Sistrurus*, native to the [[Americas]]. Its name comes from the rattle at the tail's tip, which makes a loud noise when vibrated and deters predators. Rattlesnakes are the leading contributor to snakebite injuries in North America, but they rarely bite unless provoked, and treated bites are seldom fatal. The 36 known species have between 65 and 70 subspecies. The largest, the eastern diamondback, can measure up to 2.4 m (7.9 ft). Most species live in arid regions, often near open, rocky areas. Their prey includes mice, [[Rat|rats]], [[Rabbit|rabbits]], ground squirrels and [[Prairie dog|prairie dogs]], which they kill with [[Venom|venom]]. Rattlesnakes are [[Predation|preyed on]] by hawks, [[Weasel|weasels]] and kingsnakes, especially as neonates. Many are killed by humans, and habitat destruction, poaching and extermination campaigns threaten many populations.

[[Actor|Puerto Rican actor]] and humanitarian known for intense and varied roles on stage and screen. After performing locally, he moved to New York City, where producer Joseph Papp offered him work with the New York Shakespeare Festival. In 1978 he starred opposite [[Meryl Streep]] in a revival of *The Taming of the Shrew*. He received four Tony Award nominations for Best Actor in a Musical and later starred in Broadway revivals of *Othello* (1991) and *Man of La Mancha* (1994). He gained prominence as Gomez Addams in two film adaptations of [[The Addams Family]]. He was posthumously awarded a Primetime Emmy for *The Burning Season*.

Ten-headed [[Rakshasa|rakshasa]] king of Lanka and principal antagonist of the Hindu epic *Ramayana*. In the epic he abducts [[Sita]], wife of [[Rama]], and holds her in Lanka. Rama, with the help of the vanara king Sugriva, rescues her by slaying Ravana. Ravana is also described as an ardent devotee of [[Shiva]] and a learned scholar, versed in the six shastras and the four [[Vedas]]. He is credited as the author of the *Arka Prakasha*, a Sanskrit text on [[Distillation|distillation]], and is revered in the [[Ayurveda|Ayurvedic]] tradition. Each year his defeat is celebrated by burning a large effigy during the Hindu festival of Dussehra.

City, capital of Ravenna province in [[Emilia-Romagna]], northern Italy. It came under [[Roman Republic]] control in 89 BC and became a seaport on the [[Adriatic Sea|Adriatic]]. In the fifth century, Western Roman emperor Honorius moved his court there, and the city served as capital of the Western Roman Empire for most of that century. After the empire's collapse in 476, Ravenna was ruled by the Ostrogoth king [[Theodoric the Great|Theodoric]], then conquered by the [[Byzantine Empire|Byzantines]] in 540. It later passed to the [[Papal States]] and in the mid-19th century became part of the [[Kingdom of Italy]]. Eight late Roman and Byzantine buildings form a UNESCO [[World Heritage Site]], "Early Christian Monuments of Ravenna."

Indian sitarist and composer and a leading exponent of [[Hindustani classical music]] in the second half of the 20th century. Born in [[Varanasi|Banaras]], he studied sitar for seven years under court musician Allauddin Khan. He composed the music for [[Satyajit Ray]]'s [[The Apu Trilogy|Apu Trilogy]] and was music director of All India Radio, New Delhi, from 1949 to 1956. From 1956 he toured Europe and America, popularizing Indian classical music through teaching and performance. His association with [[George Harrison]] of [[The Beatles]] helped popularize Indian instruments in Western pop music in the latter half of the 1960s. He won four [[Grammy Awards]], including Album of the Year for *The Concert for Bangladesh* in 1973, and was awarded India's highest civilian honor, the Bharat Ratna, in 1999. He was the father of musicians Norah Jones and Anoushka Shankar.

City in Punjab province, Pakistan (pop., 2025: 2.5 million), adjacent to the capital, [[Islamabad]]; the two are jointly known as the "twin cities." Founded in 1493 by a Gakhar chief, it remained a small town until the 18th century. After the [[East India Company]] annexed Punjab in 1849, it became the largest garrison town of the British Indian Army's Northern Command. It was granted municipal status in 1867. After Pakistan's independence on 14 August 1947, the city became home to the General Headquarters of the Pakistan Army. Rawalpindi served as secondary capital under Ayub Khan before Islamabad was established. It lies near the ancient city of Taxila, a World Heritage Site, and within the ancient region of Gandhara, which contains many Buddhist ruins.

American author and screenwriter who worked in [[Fantasy|fantasy]], [[Science fiction|science fiction]], horror and mystery. He is best known for the novel *Fahrenheit 451* (1953), set in a society where books are burned, and for the story collections *The Martian Chronicles* (1950), *The Illustrated Man* (1951) and *The October Country* (1955). Other works include the coming-of-age novel *Dandelion Wine* (1957) and the dark fantasy *Something Wicked This Way Comes* (1962). His fiction renamed Waukegan, Illinois, his childhood home, as Green Town. He wrote and consulted on screenplays and television scripts, including *Moby Dick* and *It Came from Outer Space*. Many of his works were adapted for film, television and comic books. [[The New York Times]] called him "the writer most responsible for bringing modern science fiction into the literary mainstream."

American singer, songwriter and pianist, regarded as one of the most influential musicians of the 20th century and a pioneer of [[Soul music|soul music]]. Charles lost his vision as a child, possibly due to [[Glaucoma|glaucoma]], and wore dark glasses. In the 1950s, recording for Atlantic Records, he combined blues, jazz, rhythm and blues and gospel. With ABC Records in the 1960s he helped integrate [[Country music|country music]], rhythm and blues and pop; his album *Modern Sounds in Country and Western Music* (1962) was his first to top the Billboard 200. His "Georgia on My Mind" was the first of three career No. 1 hits on the Billboard Hot 100. [[Frank Sinatra]] called him "the only true genius in show business." Charles received the Kennedy Center Honors and the National Medal of Arts, and won 17 [[Grammy Awards]]. He was among the inaugural inductees of the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 1986.

American businessman who turned [[McDonald's]] into the most successful global fast-food corporation by revenue. In 1954 he visited the San Bernardino, California, hamburger restaurant of Richard and Maurice McDonald, admired its speed and efficiency, and convinced the brothers to let him franchise the concept. He bought the brand in 1961 for $2.7 million, after several years as the brothers' franchising agent, and became owner of McDonald's Corporation, though he had not founded the company. He was president from 1955 to 1968 and drove aggressive expansion across the United States and then internationally. He owned the [[Major League Baseball|San Diego Padres]] from 1974 until his death.

[[American football|American football]] linebacker who played his entire 17-season career with the [[Baltimore]] Ravens of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He led the Ravens' defense to victory in [[Super Bowl|Super Bowl XXXV]], won NFL Defensive Player of the Year honors in 2000 and 2003, and was named Super Bowl Most Valuable Player. He accumulated 2,059 career combined tackles, including 1,568 solo tackles, both NFL records. Lewis was selected to 13 Pro Bowls and entered the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2018. In 2000 he pleaded guilty to obstruction of justice in connection with the stabbing deaths of two men; he testified as a key witness, and a jury determined the killings were acts of self-defense.

Scattering of light or other [[Electromagnetic radiation|electromagnetic radiation]] by particles much smaller than its [[Wavelength|wavelength]]. Scattering intensity is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the wavelength, so [[Blue|blue]] light scatters much more than [[Red|red]]. The effect is named after the 19th-century British physicist Lord Rayleigh (John William Strutt). It explains the blue daytime sky and the yellowish to reddish hue of the low [[Sun]] at twilight. It results from the electric polarizability of particles: the oscillating field of a light wave makes their charges move, and each particle re-radiates as a small dipole. Larger particles are treated by Mie theory. In c. 1506–1510, [[Leonardo da Vinci]] conjectured that small particles in the atmosphere gave the sky its blue hue.

Canadian actor best known for the title roles in the television dramas *Perry Mason* and *Ironside*. Early in his lengthy Hollywood film career he was usually cast as a villain, and he played the suspected murderer in Alfred Hitchcock's *Rear Window* (1954). He won Emmy Awards in 1959 and 1961 for *Perry Mason*, which he played for nine seasons (1957–1966) and reprised in 26 television movies. For *Ironside* he received six Emmy and two Golden Globe nominations. Accounts of his youth are sometimes mutually contradictory, and many details of his biography appeared unverifiable.

American-British novelist and screenwriter, a founder of the hardboiled school of [[Detective fiction|detective fiction]]. Chandler became a writer at age 44, in 1932, after losing his job as an oil company executive during the [[Great Depression]]. His first novel, *The Big Sleep*, was published in 1939. Its detective, Philip Marlowe, is considered by some to be synonymous with "private detective." Chandler published seven novels in his lifetime, including *Farewell, My Lovely* (1940), *The Lady in the Lake* (1943) and *The Long Goodbye* (1953). [[Humphrey Bogart]] played Marlowe on screen and is considered by many the quintessential Marlowe. Chandler co-adapted James M. Cain's novella into *Double Indemnity* (1944), directed by [[Billy Wilder]].

French-born American [[Industrial design|industrial designer]], called the Father of Industrial Design by the press. After serving in the French army in World War I, he arrived in New York in September 1919 and worked as a fashion illustrator for [[Vogue (magazine)|Vogue]] and as a department store window designer. His first industrial-design commission, in 1929, was a redesign of a Gestetner duplicating machine. His styling of the Coldspot refrigerator for [[Sears]] established his reputation. He designed locomotives for the Pennsylvania Railroad, including the GG1 electric. His corporate work included the Shell, Exxon, TWA and former [[BP]] logos, the Lucky Strike package and [[Coca-Cola]] vending machines and bottles. He consulted for [[NASA]] from 1963 to 1973 on habitability for Saturn-Apollo and Skylab. He appeared on the cover of [[Time (magazine)|Time]] on October 31, 1949.

Medical condition in which spasm of small arteries causes episodes of reduced blood flow, typically to the fingers. Episodes are usually triggered by cold or emotional stress and turn the affected skin white, then blue, then red as blood flow returns, with numbness or pain. Primary Raynaud's has no known cause, while secondary Raynaud's accompanies conditions such as [[Lupus]] or scleroderma and is more likely to be painful and to progress to digital ulcerations. The main treatment is avoiding the cold and stopping nicotine or other [[Stimulant|stimulants]]; calcium channel blockers and iloprost are used when that fails. About 4% of people have the condition, and both forms are more common in [[Climate|cold climates]]. It is named after the physician Auguste Gabriel Maurice Raynaud, who described it in his 1862 doctoral thesis.

Semi-synthetic [[Textile|textile]] fiber made from regenerated [[Cellulose|cellulose]], usually from [[Wood|wood]], also called viscose. French scientist Hilaire de Chardonnet patented the first commercial process, based on nitrocellulose, in 1885. English chemists Charles Frederick Cross, Edward John Bevan and Clayton Beadle patented the viscose process in 1894, naming it for the highly viscous solution involved. The viscose process, the most common method, uses alkali and carbon disulfide. The Lyocell process avoids carbon disulfide but is more expensive; it was developed in the late 1970s in response to concerns about the environmental impact of viscose. Rayon can imitate the feel of [[Silk|silk]], wool, [[Cotton|cotton]] and linen, and is woven or knitted into textiles.

Step-by-step sequence of elementary reactions by which an overall [[Chemical reaction|chemical reaction]] occurs. A mechanism is a theoretical conjecture, because the detailed steps are not observable in most cases; it is chosen because it is thermodynamically feasible and has experimental support. A complete mechanism must also explain the stereochemistry observed and the amount of each product formed. Reaction intermediates are often short-lived and sometimes can be isolated, whereas transition states are fleeting, high-energy species that cannot be isolated. Mechanisms are often inferred from [[Chemical kinetics|kinetics]]. In the oxidation of [[Carbon monoxide|carbon monoxide]] by nitrogen dioxide, the rate law r = k[NO₂]² shows that the slow, rate-determining step involves two NO₂ molecules rather than CO. In chain reactions, intermediates called chain carriers, often [[Radical (chemistry)|radicals]], generate intermediates in other steps.

Non-volatile [[Computer|computer]] memory whose data cannot be electronically modified after manufacture. ROM stores firmware, software rarely changed during the life of a system, and video games are sold on plug-in cartridges containing ROM. Strictly speaking, ROM refers to hard-wired memory such as mask ROM, an [[Integrated circuit|integrated circuit]] programmed with photomasks during manufacture, so correcting errors or updating software requires new devices. Erasable variants, including EPROM, EEPROM and flash memory, can be reprogrammed, but usually slowly and only a limited number of times. EPROM is erased with [[Ultraviolet|ultraviolet]] light; Intel introduced the 1701 EPROM in 1971. Early machines used discrete components, such as the capacitor and transformer read-only storage that [[IBM]] used for microcode in its smaller System/360 models. Unlike volatile RAM, ROM retains its data when the computer is switched off.

Taking in the sense or meaning of written symbols by sight or, in some cases, touch, as with [[Braille]]. The ability to read and write is called [[Literacy|literacy]]. For educators, reading is a multifaceted process involving word recognition, spelling, phonics, [[Vocabulary|vocabulary]], comprehension and fluency. It is generally an individual, silent activity. Major predictors of reading ability include oral language skills and phonological awareness. Reading for pleasure has been linked to progress in vocabulary and mathematics during adolescence, and sustained lifetime reading has been associated with high academic attainment. In the United States, it was reported in 2022 that less than half of adults had read a book in the past 12 months. An earlier UNESCO estimate put the number of people unable to read and write at 750 million.

Spanish professional [[Association football|football]] club based in [[Madrid]] that competes in [[La Liga]]. Founded in 1902, the club has been owned and operated by its members, and has played at the Bernabéu since 1947. It is the most decorated club in Europe, with a record 15 [[UEFA Champions League]] titles and a record 36 La Liga titles. Its Galácticos policy has signed star players such as [[Zinedine Zidane]] and [[David Beckham]], and in 2009 it signed [[Cristiano Ronaldo]] for a record-breaking £80 million. Its academy, La Fábrica, has produced players including Raúl and Iker Casillas.
